topics.title: Look-out, collision risk & steering rules
topics.summary: Maintain a proper look-out, assess constant bearing and decreasing range, make bold early alterations, and apply the give-way hierarchy.
topics.asa_note: Inland Rule 34 sound-signal intent differs from the International Rule.

questions.prompt: You are motor-sailing close-hauled on starboard tack and meet a pure sailing vessel on port tack. Who gives way?
forbidden_keywords: port tack gives way to starboard
questions.correct_explanation: A vessel under sail with its engine engaged is treated as power-driven; apply Rule 18 and keep clear of the sailing vessel.
questions.deep_remediation: Separate propulsion status from sail trim. Identify whether the engine is engaged, then apply the Rule 18 hierarchy.

questions.prompt: A ship is overtaking from astern and does not appear to be taking action. What is your response?
questions.correct_explanation: The overtaking vessel keeps clear under Rule 13. As stand-on vessel, monitor and act under Rule 17 if collision cannot otherwise be avoided.
questions.deep_remediation: Confirm the overtaking sector, maintain a lookout, and state the stand-on vessel's escalation duties.

topics.title: Restricted visibility
topics.summary: Proceed at safe speed with engines ready. No vessel is stand-on under Rule 19; do not turn to port for a target forward of the beam.
topics.asa_note: Rule 19 principles are materially the same under US Inland Rules; use the applicable local sound-signal requirements.

questions.prompt: A steady radar target is at 315° relative in dense fog. What action is prohibited for a target forward of the beam?
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 19(d) prohibits an alteration to port for a vessel detected forward of the beam, except when overtaking. Take clear avoiding action and proceed at safe speed.
questions.deep_remediation: Mark the target relative to the beam, then apply Rule 19(d) before choosing an alteration.

questions.prompt: You hear a three-blast fog signal forward of the beam. What immediate control measure is required?
questions.correct_explanation: The signal may indicate a sailing vessel, NUC, RAM, CBD, fishing vessel, or towing vessel. Reduce to the minimum speed at which the vessel can be kept on course and navigate with extreme caution.
questions.deep_remediation: Identify the signal pattern, list plausible vessel classes, then state the speed and lookout response.

topics.title: Lights, shapes & distress signals
topics.summary: Identify vessel status from prescribed lights and day shapes, including sailing, fishing, NUC, RAM, pilot, towing, and distress signals.
topics.asa_note: Light characteristics are international; check US Inland variations and local chart notes.

questions.prompt: At night you see red over green above a red sidelight. What vessel and aspect is indicated?
questions.correct_explanation: Red over green is an optional sailing-vessel light combination; the red sidelight indicates the port aspect.
questions.deep_remediation: Read masthead lights separately from sidelights, then infer vessel class and aspect.

questions.prompt: A tug and tow exceed 200 m. Which additional day shape and masthead light pattern should be considered?
questions.correct_explanation: A tow exceeding 200 m calls for three vertical masthead lights on the towing vessel and a black diamond shape; the tow also displays the prescribed diamond shape.
questions.deep_remediation: Determine whether the tow exceeds 200 m, then review the towing lights and day-shape requirements.

topics.title: True, magnetic, compass & leeway
topics.summary: Apply variation and deviation with direction-aware signs, then allow for leeway by steering into the wind from the intended water track.
topics.asa_note: Use the chart's stated variation and annual change; US chart conventions may differ by chart edition.

questions.prompt: Variation is 4°15′ W in 2020 and increases 10′ W annually. What is it in 2026?
questions.correct_explanation: Six years add 60 minutes west, giving 5°15′ W.
questions.deep_remediation: Count elapsed years and apply the stated annual change in the same direction.

questions.prompt: Convert 270°T to compass with 5°W variation and 3°E deviation, ignoring leeway for this conversion step.
questions.correct_explanation: Apply the chart's variation and vessel deviation with their stated directions: 270°T converts to 266°C.
questions.deep_remediation: Write each conversion as a separate signed step and check the add-west/subtract-east mnemonic.

topics.title: DR, EP, fixes & course to steer
topics.summary: Plot the water track from a known fix to DR, add the tidal vector to reach EP, and use the ground vector for COG and SOG.
topics.asa_note: Check chart datum and local chart conventions; COG is not the vessel's heading in a cross-current.

questions.prompt: Steer 090°T at 6 kn for one hour with a 2 kn tide setting 180°T. Describe DR, EP, and SOG.
questions.correct_explanation: The water track is 6 NM east; the tidal vector is 2 NM south. The ground speed is the vector magnitude, about 6.32 kn.
questions.deep_remediation: Draw the water and tide vectors head-to-tail, then calculate the resultant magnitude.

questions.prompt: A three-point fix forms a cocked hat beside a hazard. Which corner should guide your safe navigation?
questions.correct_explanation: Navigate from the corner closest to danger until the uncertainty is resolved.
questions.deep_remediation: Treat the cocked hat as an uncertainty area and choose the conservative corner.

topics.title: Tidal heights & under-keel clearance
topics.summary: Use the Rule of Twelfths as an estimate and calculate clearance from height of tide, charted depth or drying height, draft, and UKC.
topics.asa_note: UK Admiralty charts use LAT; US NOAA charts commonly use MLLW as chart datum.

questions.prompt: A tide rises from 1.0 m to 7.0 m. Estimate height two hours after low water using Rule of Twelfths.
questions.correct_explanation: The first two hours add 1/12 and 2/12 of the 6 m range: 1.0 + 0.5 + 1.0 = 2.5 m.
questions.deep_remediation: Calculate the range, divide it into twelfths, and sum the first two increments.

questions.prompt: A rock dries 1.8 m, draft is 2.0 m, and required UKC is 1.0 m. What height of tide is needed?
questions.correct_explanation: Required height of tide is drying height plus draft plus UKC: 1.8 + 2.0 + 1.0 = 4.8 m.
questions.deep_remediation: Add the drying height, vessel draft, and chosen under-keel clearance.

topics.title: Tidal diamonds & impossible CTS
topics.summary: Interpolate charted tidal rates and assess whether boat speed can overcome a cross-current on the required ground track.
topics.asa_note: Use the chart's tidal atlas or local stream data and account for the chart's reference port.

questions.prompt: Interpolate mid-range stream rate between 1.4 kn neaps and 2.8 kn springs.
questions.correct_explanation: The midpoint between 1.4 and 2.8 kn is 2.1 kn.
questions.deep_remediation: Find the daily range position, then interpolate linearly between the stated rates.

questions.prompt: Your boat makes 3 kn and a perpendicular cross-tide runs at 4 kn. Can you hold a straight track directly across?
questions.correct_explanation: The stream exceeds the boat speed, so a direct straight-line crossing is not achievable; wait for a tidal gate or change the passage plan.
questions.deep_remediation: Compare the cross-current with boat speed and select a safe alternative rather than promising an impossible CTS.

topics.title: Depressions & frontal passages
topics.summary: Use Buys Ballot's Law in the Northern Hemisphere and recognize typical cloud, pressure, rain, and wind changes at fronts.
topics.asa_note: Buys Ballot's Law reverses in the Southern Hemisphere.

questions.prompt: In the Northern Hemisphere, with your back to a south-westerly wind, where is the low pressure?
questions.correct_explanation: Buys Ballot's Law places the low to your left in the Northern Hemisphere, approximately northwest in this situation.
questions.deep_remediation: Place your back to the wind and apply the hemisphere-specific left/right rule.

questions.prompt: What pressure and wind clues may precede a warm front?
questions.correct_explanation: Pressure commonly falls; layered cloud thickens and wind often backs before the frontal passage.
questions.deep_remediation: Combine pressure tendency, cloud sequence, precipitation, and wind shift rather than relying on one clue.

topics.title: Sea breezes & fog formation
topics.summary: Distinguish daytime sea breeze circulation from advection fog over cold water and radiation fog over land.
topics.asa_note: Local sea-breeze strength depends on the gradient wind and coastline orientation.

questions.prompt: Why may advection fog over cold coastal water persist through midday?
questions.correct_explanation: Advection fog forms when warm moist air moves over colder water and usually persists until the air mass or wind changes.
questions.deep_remediation: Identify the air-water temperature relationship and distinguish advection from radiation fog.

questions.prompt: What local wind is likely on a sunny afternoon when the gradient wind is light?
questions.correct_explanation: Land heats faster than sea, drawing cooler marine air onshore as a sea breeze, often strongest during the afternoon.
questions.deep_remediation: Compare land and sea heating, then describe the resulting pressure circulation.

topics.title: Passage planning & pilotage
topics.summary: Appraise, plan, execute, and monitor the passage; identify hazards, tidal gates, escape routes, and pilotage transits.
topics.asa_note: ASA 106/108 practice commonly emphasizes a written float plan and leg-by-leg waypoint notes.

questions.prompt: A rear transit mark moves left of the front mark. Which side of the transit are you on and how should you correct?
questions.correct_explanation: The rear mark moving left indicates the vessel is to starboard of the transit; steer to port to regain it.
questions.deep_remediation: Read the relative motion of the rear mark, identify which side of the line you occupy, then correct toward the transit.

questions.prompt: How does a not-more-than clearing bearing help when passing an unlit hazard?
questions.correct_explanation: Maintain the bearing within the stated NMT limit so the vessel remains on the safe side of the hazard.
questions.deep_remediation: Plot or identify the danger side, state the bearing limit, and monitor it continuously.

topics.title: Tidal gates, bars & night entry
topics.summary: Assess wind-against-tide sea state, depth, visibility, and abort options before committing to a bar or restricted entrance.
topics.asa_note: Use local notices, pilot books, and forecast sources for the specific port and jurisdiction.

questions.prompt: At night, an onshore Force 6 opposes a spring ebb across a shallow bar. What is the conservative decision?
questions.correct_explanation: Wind against a strong ebb can create steep breaking seas over the bar. Stand off in safe water and wait for a suitable tide or conditions.
questions.deep_remediation: Name the wave hazard, preserve deep-water options, and choose a safer tide window.

questions.prompt: Name two passage-plan elements that help you avoid committing to an unsafe tidal gate.
questions.correct_explanation: Plan a latest safe time, escape route, and bolt hole before the gate so the crew can abort with margin.
questions.deep_remediation: List decision points and safe alternatives before entering the constrained area.

topics.title: MOB recovery & storm tactics
topics.summary: Raise the alarm, mark the casualty, assign a spotter, maneuver deliberately, and recover on the leeward side when safe.
topics.asa_note: Adapt recovery procedure to vessel, crew, sea state, and local rescue guidance.

questions.prompt: Why is a leeward-side pickup generally preferred for a person overboard?
questions.correct_explanation: A controlled leeward recovery reduces the risk of the hull being blown or drifted onto the casualty; adapt to conditions and vessel handling.
questions.deep_remediation: Describe relative wind and drift at the final approach, then identify the safer side.

questions.prompt: Name the sail and helm configuration commonly used to heave-to in a rising gale.
questions.correct_explanation: A backed headsail, eased or sheeted main, and helm set to maintain the balance can hold the vessel hove-to; practice on the specific boat.
questions.deep_remediation: Explain how the backed headsail and main balance the boat and keep a watch on lee shore and sea room.

topics.title: Anchoring scope, towing & Mayday
topics.summary: Calculate scope from bow roller to seabed at high water, rig a chafe-protected tow, and distinguish distress from urgency calls.
topics.asa_note: Follow local VHF channel and Coast Guard procedures; use the vessel's current radio license and MMSI details.

questions.prompt: Chart depth is 8 m, high-water rise is 4 m, and bow roller is 1.5 m above sea level. What is a 4:1 all-chain scope?
questions.correct_explanation: Total height is 8 + 4 + 1.5 = 13.5 m; at 4:1 the scope is 54 m, before any additional storm allowance.
questions.deep_remediation: Add chart depth, high-water rise, and bow-roller height, then multiply by the selected scope ratio.

questions.prompt: When do you use MAYDAY rather than PAN-PAN, and what information belongs in the call?
questions.correct_explanation: MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger. State vessel identity, position, nature of distress, assistance required, and people on board, then repeat key information as needed.
questions.deep_remediation: Classify the urgency, then rehearse the call information in a clear, ordered sequence.
